message.content:
# Target
The compiled C++ binary is /workspace/dataset/test5_executable .
Its source (the test driver only) is /workspace/dataset/test5.cpp :

    if (argc < 2) return 1;
    std::string url = argv[1];
    url_parser::URL parser(url);
    std::cout << parser.scheme() << std::endl;   // line 1
    std::cout << parser.host()   << std::endl;   // line 2
    std::cout << parser.port()   << std::endl;   // line 3  (an integer; -1 when absent)
    std::cout << parser.path()   << std::endl;   // line 4
    std::cout << parser.query()  << std::endl;   // line 5

So EVERY successful run prints exactly 5 newline-terminated lines. Empty fields print as empty lines.
The library source is NOT available and you must NOT try to find or read it. Pure black-box probing.

# How to probe (IMPORTANT)
Run it like:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'THE_URL'
To see exact bytes including empty trailing lines, ALWAYS capture with a delimiter, e.g.:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'http://a.com' | sed -n 'l' ; echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
or the most reliable formatting for reporting — number every line:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'http://a.com' | cat -A | nl -ba
Use single quotes around the URL. For URLs containing single quotes, control characters, or
non-UTF8 bytes, use perl to exec with an exact argv, e.g.:
    perl -e 'exec("/workspace/dataset/test5_executable", "http://a\x27b.com")' | cat -A | nl -ba
Batch many probes in ONE bash call with a loop so you use few tool calls, e.g.:
    for u in 'http://a' 'http://a:1' 'a://b'; do printf '=== [%s]\n' "$u"; /workspace/dataset/test5_executable "$u" | cat -A | nl -ba; done
`cat -A` renders end-of-line as `$`, tabs as `^I`, so an empty field shows as a line containing only `$`.
Probe generously — dozens to hundreds of inputs. It is cheap. Note python3 is NOT installed; perl is.
Do not write anything into /workspace/dataset or /output. Use /tmp for scratch files.

# What to report
Report the OBSERVED FACTS, not guesses. For each rule you state, cite at least one concrete
input and its exact 5 field values. If two plausible rules both explain your data, say so and
design a discriminating probe, then run it. Be exhaustive within your assigned dimension.


Dimension: PATH extraction.
Determine exactly where the path starts and ends, and whether the leading '/' is included.
Probe at minimum: 'http://a.com' (empty path?), 'http://a.com/', 'http://a.com/p',
'http://a.com/p/q/', 'http://a.com//p', 'http://a.com/p?q=1', 'http://a.com/p#f',
'http://a.com/p?q=1#f', 'http://a.com?q=1' (path empty when query directly follows host?),
'http://a.com#f', 'http://a.com:80/p', 'http://a.com/p q', 'http://a.com/a?b?c',
'http://a.com/./../x' (any normalization? probably none — verify), 'http://a.com/%2e%2e/x',
'http://a.com/p%20q' (any percent-decoding? verify), 'http://a.com/a#b?c'
(is a '?' AFTER a '#' still treated as the query start?), 'http://a.com/p;params',
'a.com/p' (no scheme — is 'a.com/p' host+path or all path?), '/just/a/path',
'http://a.com/very/long/'+many segments. Also whether the path retains a trailing slash.
Report the exact delimiter set that terminates the path and their precedence.

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

rules.rule: The path INCLUDES its leading '/'. The path is the substring starting at the first '/' that appears after the authority (i.e. after the "://" separator), and it runs to the end of the string or to the first path-terminating delimiter, whichever comes first.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com/p' -> scheme=[http] host=[a.com] port=[-1] path=[/p] query=[]. 'http://a.com/p/q/' -> path=[/p/q/].

rules.rule: Path is EMPTY (empty line 4) whenever the authority is not followed by a '/'. There is no synthesis of a default "/".
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com' -> scheme=[http] host=[a.com] port=[-1] path=[] query=[]. 'http://a.com:80' -> path=[] port=[80]. 'http://' -> path=[]. 'x://' -> path=[].

rules.rule: A bare '/' after the host yields path exactly "/" (one character).
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com/' -> path=[/] query=[]. 'x:///' -> scheme=[x] host=[] path=[/].

rules.rule: Exactly two characters terminate the path: '?' and '#'. A byte-by-byte sweep of all bytes 1..126 (except \n) placed inside a path ('http://a.com/pXq') showed only byte 35 ('#') and byte 63 ('?') changed the result; every other byte, including ':', '@', '\\', ';', '%', '+', '&', '=', space, tab, CR, DEL and high bytes, is retained verbatim inside the path.
rules.evidence: Sweep output: only 'SPECIAL byte 35 [#] path=[/p] query=[]' and 'SPECIAL byte 63 [?] path=[/p] query=[q]' deviated; e.g. 'http://a.com/p;params' -> path=[/p;params], 'http://a.com/p q' -> path=[/p q], 'http://a.com/p:1' -> path=[/p:1], 'http://a.com/p@q' -> path=[/p@q], 'http://a.com\\p' (backslash) -> host=[a.com\p] path=[] (backslash not a delimiter at all).

rules.rule: Delimiter precedence: '#' is processed FIRST on the entire raw input — everything from the first '#' onward is discarded before anything else is parsed. Then '?' splits the surviving prefix into path-part and query. Consequently a '?' that appears AFTER a '#' is NOT a query start; the query is empty.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com/a#b?c' -> path=[/a] query=[] (the '?' after '#' is ignored). Contrast 'http://a.com/a?b#c' -> path=[/a] query=[b]. Also 'http://a.com/p#q?r#s' -> path=[/p] query=[]; 'http://a.com/p?q#r?s#t' -> path=[/p] query=[q].

rules.rule: The '#' truncation and '?' split happen on the WHOLE input string BEFORE the scheme/authority are located. So a '#' or '?' occurring inside what looks like the scheme destroys scheme/host detection and the surviving prefix becomes the path.
rules.evidence: 'ht#tp://a.com/p' -> scheme=[] host=[] port=[-1] path=[ht] query=[]. 'ht?tp://a.com/p' -> scheme=[] host=[] path=[ht] query=[tp://a.com/p]. 'http#://a.com/p' -> path=[http] query=[]. 'http?://a.com/p' -> path=[http] query=[://a.com/p]. 'http#x://a.com/p' -> path=[http].

rules.rule: When the (post-fragment, post-query) string contains NO "://", there is no scheme and no host, and the ENTIRE remaining string becomes the path — including any host-looking prefix, colons, and leading double slashes.
rules.evidence: 'a.com/p' -> scheme=[] host=[] port=[-1] path=[a.com/p] query=[]. 'a.com:80/p' -> path=[a.com:80/p]. '//a.com/p' -> path=[//a.com/p]. 'http:/a.com/p' -> path=[http:/a.com/p]. 'http:a.com/p' -> path=[http:a.com/p]. 'mailto:x@y.z' -> path=[mailto:x@y.z]. 'p' -> path=[p]. '/just/a/path' -> path=[/just/a/path].

rules.rule: In the no-scheme case the path still stops at '?'/'#' with the same precedence, and does not need to start with '/'.
rules.evidence: 'a.com/p?q=1' -> path=[a.com/p] query=[q=1]. 'a.com/p#f' -> path=[a.com/p] query=[]. 'a.com?q=1' -> path=[a.com] query=[q=1]. 'a.com#f' -> path=[a.com] query=[]. '/p?q=1' -> path=[/p] query=[q=1]. 'a/b?x://y' -> path=[a/b] query=[x://y].

rules.rule: Path is empty when a query or fragment directly follows the host (no '/' present).
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com?q=1' -> path=[] query=[q=1]. 'http://a.com#f' -> path=[] query=[]. 'http://a.com#/p' -> path=[] query=[] (the '/p' after '#' is discarded, NOT treated as path). 'http://a.com?q=1#f/g' -> path=[] query=[q=1].

rules.rule: An empty query or empty fragment marker does not alter the path; the path simply ends at the marker.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com/?' -> path=[/] query=[]. 'http://a.com/#' -> path=[/] query=[]. 'http://a.com/p?' -> path=[/p]. 'http://a.com/p#' -> path=[/p]. 'http://a.com/?#' -> path=[/]. 'http://a.com/#?' -> path=[/].

rules.rule: NO path normalization whatsoever: '.', '..', empty segments, and duplicate slashes are all preserved byte-for-byte.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com/./../x' -> path=[/./../x]. 'http://a.com/a/./b/../c' -> path=[/a/./b/../c]. 'http://a.com/..' -> path=[/..]. 'http://a.com/.' -> path=[/.]. 'http://a.com//p' -> path=[//p]. 'http://a.com/a//b///c' -> path=[/a//b///c]. 'http://a.com///' -> path=[///].

rules.rule: NO percent-decoding of the path; percent sequences (including encoded delimiters) pass through literally, and a lone '%' is fine.

rules.rule: Trailing slashes are ALWAYS retained (never stripped), including multiple trailing slashes, and are retained when a query/fragment follows.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com/p/q/' -> path=[/p/q/]. 'http://a.com/p//' -> path=[/p//]. 'http://a.com/p/?q' -> path=[/p/] query=[q]. 'http://a.com/p/#f' -> path=[/p/]. 'http://a.com/a/b/c/.../z/' -> path=[/a/b/c/d/e/f/g/h/i/j/k/l/m/n/o/p/q/r/s/t/u/v/w/x/y/z/].

rules.rule: Path case is preserved exactly (no lowercasing) — unlike the scheme, which is lowercased.
rules.evidence: 'HTTP://A.COM/ABC' -> scheme=[http] host=[A.COM] path=[/ABC]. 'http://a.com/ABC/DeF' -> path=[/ABC/DeF]. 'HTTP:/ABC/def' -> path=[HTTP:/ABC/def] (case kept even in the whole-string-is-path branch).

'http://a.com/p\xffq' -> path=[/pM-^?q]. 'http://a.com/p\nq' -> 6 output lines: 3=[-1], 4=[/p], 5=[q], 6=[] i.e. path contains the raw LF.

rules.rule: The authority/path boundary is the first '/' only — '@' (userinfo) and ':' (port) are consumed inside the authority and never start the path; '@' and ':' occurring after that first '/' are ordinary path characters.
rules.evidence: Authority byte sweep 'http://hXrest': only '/' produced a nonempty path (path=[/rest]); ':' gave host=[h] path=[], '@' gave host=[rest] path=[], all other bytes gave host=[hXrest] path=[]. 'http://user:pass@a.com:8080/p/q?r=1#f' -> scheme=[http] host=[a.com] port=[8080] path=[/p/q] query=[r=1]. 'http://a.com/u@b.com/x' -> host=[a.com] path=[/u@b.com/x].

rules.rule: Only the FIRST "://" delimits the scheme; any later "://" is ordinary text, so a second "://" inside the authority region makes the path begin with '//'.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com://b/c' -> scheme=[http] host=[a.com] port=[-1] path=[//b/c]. 'a://b://c/d' -> scheme=[a] host=[b] path=[//c/d]. 'a://b/c://d' -> scheme=[a] host=[b] path=[/c://d]. 'http:://a.com/p' -> scheme=[http:] host=[a.com] path=[/p]. 'http://a.com/http://b.com/x' -> path=[/http://b.com/x].

rules.rule: An empty scheme (input begins with "://") still activates the authority branch, so the path still starts at the first '/' after the authority.
rules.evidence: '://a.com/p' -> scheme=[] host=[a.com] port=[-1] path=[/p] query=[]. '://p' -> host=[p] path=[]. '://' -> host=[] path=[].

rules.rule: Path length is unbounded in practice and copied exactly (no truncation).
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com' + '/x' repeated 2500 times + '?q=1' -> 5 lines, path length 5000, byte-identical to the input path, query=[q=1].

rules.rule: Consistent overall pipeline that explains every observation: (1) drop everything from the first '#' of the raw string; (2) if a '?' remains, query = text after the first '?', keep the prefix; (3) find the first "://" in that prefix — if absent, scheme=host="", path = whole prefix; (4) otherwise scheme = lowercase(text before "://"), then in the remainder find the first '/': text before it is the authority (userinfo/host/port), and path = that '/' through the end of the prefix (empty if no '/'). Nothing is decoded, normalized, trimmed, or case-folded in the path.
rules.evidence: Cross-checks: 'ht?tp://a.com/p' -> path=[ht] query=[tp://a.com/p] (steps 1-3 precede scheme detection); 'http://a.co?m/p' -> host=[a.co] path=[] query=[m/p]; 'http://a.com/a/b?c/d#e/f' -> path=[/a/b] query=[c/d]; 'http://a.com://b/c' -> path=[//b/c]; 'http://a.com' -> path=[].

observations.input: http://a.com/pXq sweep, X = each byte 1..126 (except LF)
observations.note: proves path terminator set is exactly {'?','#'}

uncertainties: A NUL byte cannot be tested because argv strings are NUL-terminated: 'http://a.com/p\x00q' yielded path=[/p], which only shows the C-string truncation, not library behavior.

Whether the implementation literally erases the fragment first and then splits on '?' (my stated pipeline) versus computing the '#' index and the '?' index up front and requiring the '?' index to be less than the '#' index. Both explain 100% of observed data ('http://a.com/a#b?c' -> path=/a query=empty; 'ht?tp://a.com/p' -> path=ht query=tp://a.com/p) and are behaviorally indistinguishable from the outside, so this is a code-shape ambiguity only, not a behavioral one.

Whether the path start is found as "first '/' in the post-scheme remainder" versus "first '/' at or after the index of "://"+3 in the pre-query string" — indistinguishable, since the scheme portion before the first "://" can never contain a '/' that precedes it in a way that differs (probe 'a://b://c/d' -> path=//c/d is consistent with both).
No upper bound on path length was found (5000-char path round-tripped exactly); a limit above that was not searched for.

Behavior for paths containing bytes that form invalid UTF-8 in the middle of a multibyte sequence was only spot-checked (single 0xFF and a valid 3-byte UTF-8 char); both passed through unchanged, so no validation appears to exist, but the whole 128..255 range was not swept in the path position.
